# SK1132 — A named tuple element is reached by its position

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`t.Item1` where the tuple's first element is called `Count`: the name that would tell the reader what the value is sits in the type and is not used.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | 7.0 |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

A model that has just written `(int Count, string Name)` and consumes the value a few lines later falls back on `Item1`/`Item2`, the `System.Tuple`-era spelling that dominates its training data. `r.Item1` compiles, is correct, and tells the reader nothing, while the name that would have told them sits in the signature. The element's name and `ItemN` are two fields over one storage slot of one `ValueTuple`, so the fix is a rename of one written token and changes no program.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var r = Get(); // (int Count, string Name)
return r.Item2 + ": " + r.Item1;
```

Write:

```csharp
var r = Get(); // (int Count, string Name)
return r.Name + ": " + r.Count;
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The name is read off the type of the receiver at this site, never off the value.** `(int X, int Y) b = a;` where `a` is `(int A, int B)` is one value with two sets of names, and only `b`'s own type says what may follow `b.` — so `b.Item1` becomes `b.X`. The rule takes the containing type of the field `Item1` binds to, which is exactly that type. ⚠ **Declared names only; an inferred name is declined, and this used to say the two cannot be told apart.** Since C# 7.1 `var t = (low, high);` gives `t` the type `(int low, int high)`, and `IsExplicitlyNamedTupleElement` answers `true` for `low` — but the element's location tells them apart: a declared name sits on a `TupleElementSyntax` or a `name:`, an inferred one on the literal's bare argument, and a name from `TupleElementNamesAttribute` has no source location and is always declared. An inferred name is the spelling of an argument, not a declaration: Vixen's `var value = ((int)x, flipped, (int)width, (int)height);` would have read the slot its field calls `Y` as `value.flipped`, beside elements with no name at all — all four of the first Vixen findings were this shape (recovered from the abandoned `stuff` branch's SK1074 measurement). ⚠ **`Item8` and beyond are rewritten to the right name.** In metadata the eighth element lives in `Rest.Item1`, but the semantic model binds `t.Item8` to a field of the full tuple type and its element list is flat, so the name is taken from the eighth position, not the first of `Rest`. `t.Rest.Item1` is a different expression whose receiver is an unnamed `ValueTuple<…>`, and is silent. Not reported: an unnamed tuple; a position a partially named tuple leaves unnamed; an element literally named `Item1` at position 1; `System.Tuple<…>.Item1`, a property with one name; a `dynamic` receiver; a tuple from metadata without `TupleElementNamesAttribute`; a struct or interface that merely has an `Item1` member. ⚠ `nameof(t.Item1)` is the string `"Item1"`, so renaming inside it changes a value; it is declined. A documentation `cref` has no receiver and is not reached. ⚠ **Writes are reported too** — `t.Item1 = 5`, `t.Item1++`, compound assignment, `ref t.Item1` and `out t.Item1` all name the same field, and the rename is the same edit. ⚠ **`SK1070` owns one shape both rules see.** A complete run of `var x = t.ItemK;` declarations reading every element of a named tuple once, in order, is `SK1070`'s deconstruction; this rule's rename would land inside the lines `SK1070` replaces, and applied first it would turn the reads into `t.Low`, which `SK1070` no longer recognises. Those reads are left to `SK1070`, so with `SK1070` switched off they are reported by neither rule. ⚠ **The fix is proved to bind back, not assumed to.** The compiler forbids the element names that would collide with `ValueTuple`'s own members (CS8125, CS8126), but `GetType` is not on that list; the rule asks member lookup that the new name is exactly the element, and binds the renamed access speculatively to confirm it reaches the same positional field. A reserved keyword name such as `@class` is written with its `@`. **Not reached:** a property pattern `{ Item1: 1 }` and a `with` initializer `{ Item1 = 1 }`, which name the member without a receiver expression.
